svg.aria-label: A diagram showing why, for transparent biological specimens, the class label is carried by the optical phase rather than by brightness. The first panel shows a conventional brightfield capture of an unstained cell, which is nearly invisible because the cell absorbs almost no light: the amplitude channel is close to empty and a classifier trained on it has almost no signal. The second panel shows the same cell as a quantitative phase map, where each pixel reports the optical path difference the light accumulated passing through it; this is proportional to integrated refractive index, which is in turn proportional to the cell's dry mass, so the phase image is a physical measurement in picograms rather than an arbitrary intensity, and morphology, mass and internal structure all become measurable. The third panel shows a three-dimensional refractive index tomogram built from many illumination angles, which resolves organelles, but it is missing a cone of spatial frequencies along the optical axis because no illumination angle can capture them, so axial resolution is systematically worse and the reconstruction must be regularized. A band at the bottom shows the wrapped phase problem: the measured phase is only known modulo two pi, so a smooth physical thickness appears as a sawtooth with artificial discontinuities, and a real-valued convolutional network reads those wrap edges as real object edges unless the phase is unwrapped first or the network is made complex-valued.
svg.title: Phase as the class label: an empty amplitude channel, a quantitative phase map, a refractive-index tomogram, and the wrapping problem
svg.text: Where the class label actually lives: amplitude is nearly empty, phase is a physical measurement
An unstained cell is a phase object: it barely absorbs light, but it delays it. Recovering that delay is what makes label-free classification possible at all.

g.text: 1 · amplitude channel — brightfield
transmitted intensity |U|² ≈ constant
contrast ≈ 1–2%: the object is there,
but almost nothing was absorbed.
the usual fix is to destroy the sample
Stains and fluorescent labels add contrast, but
they are toxic, photobleach, and take hours of
prep — so you cannot watch the same live cell
for a day, and you cannot do it at flow rates.
2 · phase channel — quantitative phase (QPI)
high OPD
low OPD
φ(x,y) = (2π/λ) · ∫ Δn(x,y,z) dz
optical path difference → integrated
refractive index → dry mass in picograms
the pixel value has physical units
Unlike an RGB intensity, φ is calibrated and
instrument-independent. Two labs’ phase maps of
the same cell should agree in value — a much
stronger basis for transfer than a stain intensity.
3 · 3D refractive index — holotomography
many illumination angles
n(x,y,z): nucleoli, lipid droplets, mitochondria
the missing cone
No illumination angle reaches
these axial frequencies — ever.
axial resolution is structurally worse
The tomogram is not an under-sampled volume that
more data would fix; a whole band of frequencies is
absent. Whatever fills it — a prior, a regularizer, a
diffusion model — is inference, not measurement.
… and the phase you measure is not the phase you want: it is known only modulo 2π
true optical thickness
what the sensor reports (wrapped)
why this breaks an ordinary CNN
Those vertical jumps are not object boundaries — they are an
artefact of arctangent. A real-valued edge-sensitive network reads
them as structure. Fix: unwrap first, or go complex-valued.
